question: Under Texas's community property system, property acquired by either spouse during marriage is presumed to be:
choice_a: Automatically the separate property of whichever spouse's name is on the title
choice_b: Jointly owned only if both spouses' names appear on the deed
choice_c: Community property, unless proven to be separate property by clear and convincing evidence
choice_d: Automatically split 50/50 into each spouse's separate estate at acquisition
explanation: Texas Family Code Section 3.003 establishes a presumption that property possessed by either spouse during or on dissolution of marriage is community property, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence that the property is separate (such as property owned before marriage or acquired by gift or inheritance).
source_note: Texas Family Code Section 3.001 et seq. & 3.101 et seq. (Community Property), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: The sale of a married couple's homestead property in Texas generally requires:
choice_a: Only the signature of the spouse whose name appears on the deed
choice_b: No spousal signature requirement under any circumstance
choice_c: Court approval in every homestead sale, regardless of spousal agreement
choice_d: Both spouses' joinder/signature, even if the property is titled in only one spouse's name
explanation: Texas homestead protections generally require both spouses to join in conveying homestead property, reflecting the Texas Constitution's strong protection of the family home regardless of which spouse holds record title.
source_note: Texas Family Code Section 5.001 et seq. (Sale of Homestead Community Property); Texas Constitution Article 16, Sections 50-51, Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: The Texas Constitution's homestead protections primarily shield a homeowner's residence from:
choice_a: Forced sale by most general creditors, subject to specific statutory exceptions
choice_b: All property taxes forever
choice_c: Any future sale by the owner
choice_d: Zoning regulation entirely
explanation: The Texas Constitution's homestead exemption (Article 16, Sections 50-52) protects a homeowner's residence from forced sale by most general creditors, with specific enumerated exceptions such as purchase-money liens, tax liens, home equity loans, and mechanic's liens for home improvements.
source_note: Texas Constitution Article 16, Sections 50-52 (Homestead), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas homeowner's residence homestead qualifies for a reduction in taxable assessed value for school district and other property taxes under which provision?
choice_a: Tax Code Section 34.21 exclusively
choice_b: Tax Code Section 11.13 (residence homestead exemption)
choice_c: Business and Commerce Code Section 17.46
choice_d: Property Code Section 92.001
explanation: Tax Code Section 11.13 establishes the general residence homestead exemption, reducing the taxable assessed value of an owner's primary residence for ad valorem tax purposes, with additional exemptions available under related sections for over-65, disabled, and veteran homeowners.
source_note: Texas Tax Code Sections 11.13, 11.41, 11.43 (Homestead), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A former property owner whose home was sold at a tax foreclosure sale in Texas may, under limited circumstances, exercise a statutory:
choice_a: Automatic reinstatement with no payment required
choice_b: Permanent bar from ever repurchasing the property
choice_c: Right of redemption, allowing repurchase within a specified period after the tax sale
choice_d: Right to void the sale for any reason at any time with no deadline
explanation: Tax Code Section 34.21 gives certain former owners (notably homestead, agricultural, or mineral interest owners) a statutory right of redemption allowing repurchase of tax-sale property within a specified period by paying the purchaser's costs plus a statutory premium.
source_note: Texas Tax Code Section 34.21 (Right of Redemption), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: The Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act (DTPA) is codified within which statute?
choice_a: Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1101
choice_b: Texas Property Code Chapter 92
choice_c: Texas Family Code Chapter 3
choice_d: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sections 17.42-17.50
explanation: The DTPA, at Business and Commerce Code Sections 17.42-17.50 (also commonly cited around Sections 17.41-17.63), prohibits false, misleading, or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce, and has been used against real estate licensees for material misrepresentations or nondisclosures in transactions.
source_note: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sections 17.42-17.50 (Deceptive Trade Practices Act), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas resident who dies intestate (without a valid will), leaving no surviving spouse but survived by children, generally has their property distributed:
choice_a: According to the law of descent and distribution set out in the Texas Estates Code
choice_b: Entirely to the state through escheat, regardless of surviving heirs
choice_c: According to whatever verbal wishes the decedent expressed to family members
choice_d: Equally to the decedent's closest friends, ahead of any children
explanation: Texas Estates Code Section 201 governs intestate succession, setting out a statutory hierarchy for distributing a decedent's property among surviving heirs (spouse, children, parents, siblings, etc.) when no valid will exists.
source_note: Texas Estates Code Section 201 (Descent and Distribution, Intestate Succession), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas residential landlord's right to seize and hold a tenant's nonexempt personal property left on the premises for unpaid rent, when properly provided for in the lease, is called a:
choice_a: Mechanic's lien
choice_b: Residential landlord's lien
choice_c: Judgment lien
choice_d: Tax lien
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 54.041 et seq. governs the residential landlord's lien, allowing a landlord with a properly disclosed contractual lien in the lease to seize nonexempt tenant property for unpaid rent, subject to strict statutory procedural requirements and notice obligations.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 54.041 et seq. (Residential Landlord Lien), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: The Texas Property Code chapter most directly governing residential landlord-tenant relationships, including security deposits and the landlord's duty to repair, is:
choice_a: Chapter 5
choice_b: Chapter 41
choice_c: Chapter 92
choice_d: Chapter 13
explanation: Property Code Chapter 92 governs Texas residential landlord-tenant relationships, addressing security deposit handling and refund deadlines, the landlord's duty to repair conditions materially affecting health/safety, smoke detector requirements, and related tenant remedies.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 92.001 (Landlord-Tenant Issues), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A lender pursuing foreclosure on a Texas residential mortgage secured by a deed of trust with a power-of-sale clause most commonly proceeds through:
choice_a: Judicial foreclosure exclusively, since Texas prohibits non-judicial foreclosure
choice_b: A separate federal foreclosure proceeding
choice_c: TREC administrative action
choice_d: Non-judicial foreclosure under Property Code Section 51.002
explanation: Property Code Section 51.002 governs the streamlined non-judicial foreclosure process used for the vast majority of Texas deed-of-trust foreclosures, requiring notice of default, notice of sale posted and filed at least 21 days before the sale, and a public sale on the first Tuesday of the month.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 51.002 et seq. (Foreclosures), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas real property recording statute generally protects a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value against:
choice_a: Prior unrecorded conveyances or liens the purchaser had no actual or constructive notice of
choice_b: Every prior claim regardless of recording or notice
choice_c: Nothing; Texas has no recording statute protections
choice_d: Only claims arising after the purchaser's own purchase
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 13.001 et seq. establishes the recording statute framework, generally protecting a bona fide purchaser who pays value without notice of a prior unrecorded conveyance or lien against that prior, unrecorded claim -- underscoring why title searches and prompt recording matter so much in practice.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 13.001 et seq. (Recording Statutes), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas contractor who is not paid for labor or materials furnished to improve real property may secure payment by filing a:
choice_a: Homestead exemption claim
choice_b: Mechanic's, contractor's, or materialman's lien against the improved property
choice_c: Recovery Trust Account claim
choice_d: TREC complaint against the property owner
explanation: Texas law (commonly summarized under mechanic's and materialman's lien provisions) allows unpaid contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers who furnish labor or materials for property improvements to secure a lien against the improved property, subject to strict notice and filing deadlines -- and subject to Texas's constitutional homestead protections limiting such liens on homestead property to certain contractually pre-agreed improvement liens.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VI.H (Mechanic's and Materialman's Liens), Pearson VUE #094401

question: The Texas Veterans Land Board (VLB) primarily provides which benefit relevant to real estate practice?
choice_a: Direct grants of land title to any Texas resident regardless of veteran status
choice_b: Regulatory oversight of real estate licensing in Texas
choice_c: Land, home, and home improvement loan programs available to eligible Texas veterans, often at favorable terms
choice_d: Administration of the Real Estate Recovery Trust Account
explanation: The Texas Veterans Land Board administers land, home purchase, and home improvement loan programs specifically for eligible Texas veterans, a distinctly Texas-specific benefit program that brokers working with veteran clients should be familiar with.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VI.I (Veterans Land Board), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A Texas homeowners association's authority to enforce recorded deed restrictions and assess fees against homeowners is generally addressed under the Texas Property Code provisions governing:
choice_a: Only federal fair housing law
choice_b: The state's mechanic's lien statute exclusively
choice_c: TREC's licensing chapter, with no separate HOA statute
choice_d: Restrictive covenants and property owners' associations
explanation: Texas Property Code provisions addressing restrictive covenants and property owners' associations govern an HOA's authority to enforce recorded deed restrictions, levy assessments, and, in some circumstances, place liens on non-paying members' property, a body of law distinct from TREC's broker/agent licensing framework.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VI.J (Home Owners Associations), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A buyer who has signed a purchase contract but has not yet closed holds an 'equitable interest' in the property, meaning that interest:
choice_a: Is a real, protectable interest recognized under Texas law even before legal title formally transfers at closing
choice_b: Has no legal significance whatsoever until the deed is recorded
choice_c: Is identical in every respect to holding full legal title
choice_d: Automatically extinguishes if the seller changes their mind before closing
explanation: Texas law recognizes a contract purchaser's equitable interest as a real, protectable property interest arising from a valid, binding purchase contract -- distinct from, but legally meaningful alongside, the seller's continuing legal title until closing actually occurs.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VI.K (Equitable Interest), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A Texas seller facing an imminent foreclosure who sells the property for less than the outstanding loan balance, with the lender's agreement to accept the reduced payoff, has completed a:
choice_a: Standard cash sale with no lender involvement
choice_b: Short sale
choice_c: Contract for deed
choice_d: Tax sale
explanation: A short sale occurs when a distressed seller's lender agrees to accept less than the full outstanding loan balance to allow a sale to proceed, avoiding the more damaging foreclosure process for both the borrower's credit and the lender's ultimate recovery.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VI.F (Foreclosure and Short Sales), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A Texas married couple wishes to sell property that one spouse owned individually before the marriage (separate property). This sale generally:
choice_a: Never requires the other spouse's signature under any circumstance
choice_b: Automatically converts the property to community property upon marriage
choice_c: May require the other spouse's joinder if the property is the couple's homestead, even though it remains that spouse's separate property
choice_d: Can never be sold once the couple marries
explanation: Even separate property retains its separate character despite marriage, but if that separate property also serves as the couple's homestead, Texas homestead law still generally requires both spouses' joinder to convey it -- illustrating how community property and homestead protections operate as related but distinct legal concepts.
source_note: Texas Family Code Section 3.001 et seq. (Community Property); Texas Constitution Article 16, Sections 50-51 (Homestead), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A rental income stream generated by a Texas spouse's separately owned rental property during the marriage is generally treated, absent an agreement otherwise, as:
choice_a: Automatically separate property, following the character of the underlying asset
choice_b: Property belonging solely to whichever spouse manages the rental
choice_c: Not subject to any community/separate property characterization at all
choice_d: Community property, even though the underlying rental property itself remains separate property
explanation: Under Texas community property law, income generated by separate property during the marriage (such as rents, dividends, and interest) is generally itself community property, even though the underlying asset producing that income remains the owning spouse's separate property -- an important and commonly tested distinction.
source_note: Texas Family Code Section 3.001 et seq. (Community Property); Pearson VUE #094400 sample question 43

question: A Texas seller who has not yet given a required disclosure related to a property's proximity to a hazardous natural resource, such as certain oil/gas or coastal conditions, and later faces a buyer's claim, is most likely to encounter which body of law layered on top of the general Property Code Section 5.008 disclosure?
choice_a: The Natural Resources Code's specific coastal and resource-related seller disclosure provisions
choice_b: Only federal environmental law, with no Texas-specific overlay
choice_c: No additional disclosure obligation exists beyond Property Code Section 5.008
choice_d: The Texas Business Organizations Code
explanation: Texas layers specific, additional disclosure obligations under the Natural Resources Code (coastal areas, certain resource conditions) and the Water Code (water district notices) on top of the general Property Code Section 5.008 Seller's Disclosure Notice, meaning brokers must check for these narrower, property-specific disclosure triggers beyond the standard form.
source_note: Texas Natural Resources Code Sections 33.135, 61.025; Texas Water Code Section 49.452, Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas landlord's failure to timely refund a residential tenant's security deposit or provide an itemized list of deductions, as required by Property Code Chapter 92, exposes the landlord to:
choice_a: No consequence, since security deposit handling is unregulated in Texas
choice_b: Statutory penalties, including the possibility of the tenant recovering the deposit plus a statutory penalty and attorney's fees
choice_c: Criminal prosecution only, with no civil remedy available to the tenant
choice_d: Automatic loss of the landlord's real estate license, even for a non-licensee landlord
explanation: Property Code Chapter 92 requires landlords to refund security deposits (less lawful deductions) within a statutory deadline and provide an itemized accounting; a landlord who acts in bad faith by failing to comply can be liable to the tenant for the deposit, a statutory penalty, and attorney's fees.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 92.001 et seq. (Landlord-Tenant), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources

question: A Texas homeowner's residence homestead is protected from most creditor claims, but this protection generally does NOT extend to which of the following?
choice_a: Any lien whatsoever, since homestead protection is absolute
choice_b: Claims from the homeowner's unsecured credit card debt
choice_c: A purchase-money mortgage lien or a properly created home equity/home improvement lien on the property
choice_d: Claims from a personal injury judgment unrelated to the property
explanation: The Texas Constitution enumerates specific, limited exceptions to homestead protection, including purchase-money liens, ad valorem tax liens, home equity loan liens, and certain mechanic's/materialman's liens for home improvements -- ordinary unsecured debts and unrelated judgments generally cannot reach homestead property.
source_note: Texas Constitution Article 16, Sections 50-52 (Homestead), Pearson VUE #094400 study resources
